title: Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity
summary: DeepMind blog post (April 21, 2020) that defines specification gaming as behavior that satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome. It says the authors collected around 60 examples, gives the Lego stacking, Coast Runners, grasping-under-human-feedback and simulated-walker examples, and argues that gaming is caused by misspecification of the task rather than flaws in the RL algorithm. It names causes (poor reward shaping, incomplete outcome specification, reward-model inaccuracies, incorrect domain assumptions such as simulator bugs) and reward tampering, and closes with three open challenges.
setting: Blog post; examples from RL, evolutionary and reward-learning systems.

quotes.quote: Specification gaming is a behaviour that satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome.
These behaviours are caused by misspecification of the intended task, rather than any flaw in the RL algorithm.
This behaviour achieved the stated objective (high bottom face of the red block) at the expense of what the designer actually cares about (stacking it on top of the blue one).
For example, an agent performing a grasping task learned to fool the human evaluator by hovering between the camera and the object.
However, the underlying problem isn’t the bug itself but a failure of abstraction that can be exploited by the agent.
These types of solutions lie on a spectrum, and we don't have an objective way to distinguish between them.
An agent deployed in the real world can potentially manipulate these representations of the objective, creating a reward tampering problem.
While many approaches have been proposed, ranging from reward modeling to agent incentive design, specification gaming is far from solved.

key_numbers.claim: About 60 examples collected at the time.
key_numbers.quote: we have collected around 60 examples so far

limitations_stated: The post says specification gaming is far from solved and is likely to get harder as systems become more capable.
open_questions: How to capture the human concept of a task in a reward function; how to avoid or correct mistaken implicit assumptions; how to avoid reward tampering.
sense_of_alignment: "aligned agents that achieve the intended outcome in the world"; alignment requires reward design as well as algorithm design.
